title: Chấm điểm cha mẹ · Discuss both views
prompt: Some people support requiring new parents to attend publicly funded parenting courses, while others oppose it because of the risks it could create. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

paragraphs: Public parenting courses can offer practical help, but funding advice and compelling attendance are different decisions. I oppose compulsory courses for all new parents and favour accessible voluntary provision, with mandatory intervention confined to justified child-protection cases.

Supporters argue that accessible courses can help parents interpret unfamiliar developmental needs. Practical advice can replace inconsistent information obtained from social media. A course could demonstrate safe sleep practices and constructive responses to common childhood behaviour. Demonstrating a practice and allowing questions can make advice more usable than a generic warning, especially for parents encountering unfamiliar developmental stages.

Opponents warn that compulsory attendance may stigmatise families or ignore cultural and practical differences. Mandatory attendance imposes time and transport costs that differ across households, while a standard course may not fit every family's circumstances. Treating absence as evidence of poor parenting can stigmatise people whose main difficulty is access rather than a lack of concern for their child. Support should be welcoming and flexible, with compulsion limited to clearly justified protection cases. Flexible provision should lower practical barriers before attendance is interpreted as commitment, and any compulsion needs a protection justification beyond the general value of advice. Evening sessions, interpreters and remote questions would help parents use the advice; a missed class should trigger an offer of another appointment rather than an automatic judgement about neglect. Useful advice does not require universal compulsion, while penalties for absence can burden precisely the parents with the least control over working hours and transport.
In conclusion, the value of practical parenting guidance supports public provision, but does not justify treating attendance as a universal test of parental responsibility.
